perUnit.text: When I built Ask for the Suits & Sandals site, its writing model decided when a question needed me instead of an answer. It showed the wrong handoff card in 5 of 57 test turns.

I then ported Ask to this site. Press ⌘K anywhere, or tap Ask in the dock, and ask about my work in plain words. It answers in under 120 words, only from what is published here, and lists the pages it used. When the honest answer is "ask Miles", it says so and opens a short form that reaches me. [check: why you built Ask in the first place, in one sentence of your own]

On Suits & Sandals, a judge now makes the handoff call before the writer runs. Across the same 19 questions, three runs each, it picked the right card in all 57 turns. This post covers how a question becomes an answer, how the index keeps up with publishing, what the judge does and what it cost, and how questions are logged without keeping the people who ask them.
I build this site with AI coding agents: 261 of the repo's 486 commits are co-authored by one. [check: how design, direction, review and code were split on Ask]
Ask answers from passages of this site, and when no passage is close enough to a first question, no model runs at all. A question takes four steps:

**Embed.** OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small turns the question into a vector of 1,536 numbers. A follow-up is embedded alone and joined to the previous question. **Retrieve.** Postgres with pgvector, an extension that stores and searches vectors, returns the 12 nearest passages above a cosine similarity of 0.3, through an HNSW index. **Group.** The passages are grouped into at most four pages, three passages each. **Write.** gpt-5-mini writes the answer from those passages only, in under 120 words.
If nothing clears the 0.3 floor on a first question, the visitor gets a card offering me instead, and no model runs. A weak match never turns into a paragraph, because nothing is asked to write one.

The writer can also hand a question off. It has a handoff tool with five reasons: an estimate, a project, a person, contact details, or no answer. The model picks the reason. Every word on the card is written in code, so the text that sends a visitor to me is never improvised.
Publishing is what updates the index. It is one pgvector table, `ask_embeddings`, declared in Drizzle beside Payload's schema, and nothing outside the CMS writes to it.

An `afterChange` hook on Pages, Works, Posts and Site Info re-embeds a document when it is published. Draft saves and autosave are skipped, and an unpublish deletes the document's rows. Drafts never reach the index.

Protected client work never reaches it either, and the reason is how the indexer reads. It reads each document as an anonymous visitor would, so a protected case study fails the read and leaves nothing to retrieve.

Passages aim for 2,000 characters and are split on headings. Vectors are reused by exact passage text, so fixing an SEO title re-embeds nothing. A full rebuild of this site takes 12 seconds: 19 documents, 70 passages.

The judge sorts each turn and weighs each passage before the writer runs. It is Jev, TypeSafe's System One model, which answers typed questions (Choice, Noul, Score) with probabilities, and my code owns every threshold.

Each turn gets one Jev request. It classifies the turn as information, estimate, project, person or conversation, and asks whether the turn is about the visitor's own project and whether it names my work. Each retrieved passage gets a request of its own, asking whether it is relevant and whether it holds evidence. Code keeps a passage at 0.45 relevance and 0.55 evidence.
Those passage checks let the similarity floor drop from 0.3 to 0.2. A lower floor lets more passages through, and the thresholds drop the ones that don't belong.

Probabilities matter because a Choice will pick an option even when none fits. Asked to "fix the FAQ about pricing" on a home page with no FAQ, locateBlock, the tool that finds which block an edit means, still picked a block with a Choice, at 0.46. A Noul put the odds that any block fits at 0.02, so the tool answered none.

Measured on the Suits & Sandals site on September 19, over 57 turns (19 questions, three runs each), the judge raised the right handoff card from 52 turns to all 57. Turns answered without any writing-model call went from 6 to 23.

The judge made worded answers slower, because it runs before the writer. Median time to first output went from 3,490 ms to 4,655 ms. Setting the writer to minimal reasoning brought it to 1,542 ms. Card-only turns went from 2,669 ms to 365 ms.

On this site the judge isn't on yet. It ships behind the `ASK_JEV` switch, off for now, and shadow mode comes next. Today a grounded answer here takes 5 to 6 seconds end to end, with about 1,650 input and 300 output tokens.
Every turn is saved to an ask-questions collection with emails, phone numbers, keys and long tokens stripped out. No IP address or visitor id is kept.
Code sets each turn's outcome (answered, partial, `no_sources` or `chat_only`), not the model. That makes the content-gaps filter a real list of questions the site cannot answer yet.

Stored questions are kept 90 days, and deleting them on time took two attempts. The first was a daily cron, and it never ran. [check: why the cron never ran, if you want the reason on the page] Since October 17, nothing on this site runs on a schedule: expired rows are deleted after each stored question.

Taken together, these choices move judgment out of the writing model and into code I can read and measure: the similarity floor, the passage thresholds, the words on the card, the outcome in the log. The model still writes the answer. Whether it should write one is becoming a question with a number on it.
Press ⌘K to ask it about my work.

evidence: The pre-push hook is the one that earns its keep. It is an allowlist of schema-owning files, not whole folders, so a change to a block's component or a story never trips it and nobody learns to bypass it. When a push adds a migration, it fetches origin/dev and fails unless the branch holds every migration on dev and its own sort after dev's newest. On October 7 this site's repo took 58 commits. They came from 14 workspaces I opened that day, each on its own branch, each with its own dev server and database, most of them driven by a coding agent while I reviewed the one before. Since 25 September the count is 170 commits, 23 migrations and 37 workspace branches, from one person.

A new workspace database is a clone of the main dev database, payload, which is itself a production restore pulled by the dev TUI. So every workspace opens with real content, offline, and the clone takes about a second: CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE copies files rather than rows. Postgres refuses the template while another session is connected to it, which is whenever the main dev server is running, so the helper falls back to a dump and restore.

Ports are checked before use. Conductor reserves ten ports per workspace but never checks they are free. A dev server orphaned from another repo can still hold one, and the Open button would reach the wrong site. run-dev.sh refuses to start on a taken port and prints the owning pid and checkout.

None of that is possible with one checkout. Someone building alone is rarely blocked by how fast they can write code. They are blocked by waiting: a dev server restarting, an agent running for ten minutes, a schema push that has to finish before the next thing starts. One checkout means one branch, one port, one database. Start a second task and you stash, switch, re-sync the schema and lose the state of the first.

Two workspaces changing the schema at once is the real test of a parallel setup. The rule that makes it safe has two halves. Local databases are push-managed: on every pnpm dev, Drizzle diffs the Payload config against the workspace database and applies the difference. Neon, in preview and production, is only ever changed by payload migrate inside the Vercel build. Nothing runs migrations by hand, and push is wired so it cannot reach a remote database.

perUnit.text: More than half the commits in this site's repo list a coding agent as co-author: 261 of 486. The usual reading of a number like that is that design shrinks to a description. Say what you want, review the diff, ship. If the code arrives on its own, judgment becomes a nice extra.

My work has gone the other way. Agents made building cheap, and the cost moved to the decisions around it: what a task should be, what the system must refuse to do, and whether the result is right. Those were always design questions. Now there are more of them, and they arrive faster.

The speed is real. On 7 October this repo took 58 commits from 14 workspaces, each on its own branch, most of them driven by a coding agent while I reviewed the one before. I keep three to six open at a time, and the limit is my attention, not the machine. An agent will finish the task it was given. It won't tell me whether that was the right task, or whether "done" matches what a visitor needs.

Ask, the box on this site that answers questions about my work, shows what that judgment looks like. It answers from published pages only, in under 120 words, and lists the pages it used. The design question in Ask is when it should not answer at all: when someone wants an estimate, wants to talk about their own project, or asks something the site holds no answer to. Then the honest reply is "ask Miles", and Ask should say so and open a short form that reaches me.

Before the judge, the writing model made that call. On the Suits & Sandals site, where I built Ask first, it showed the wrong handoff card in 5 of 57 test turns (19 questions, three runs each). So a second model now classifies each turn before the writer runs, and code, not the model, owns every threshold. In the same test the right card came up 57 times out of 57. Every word on those cards is written in code as well. That choice fixes what a visitor reads at the moment they want a person.

The judge had a price. It runs before the writer, so worded answers got slower: median time to first output went from 3,490 ms to 4,655 ms, until setting the writer to minimal reasoning brought it to 1,542 ms. On this site the judge still ships switched off, with shadow mode next. I decided what Ask refuses and where its thresholds sit, and coding agents built much of it under my review. [check: how the Ask work was split between Miles and the agents; no source records it]

The same judgment runs through work no visitor sees. The scripts that give each workspace its own database and port are short. The guards around them took longer to write, and each one came after a bug: a renamed workspace that spun up a second database, a dev server from another repo holding a port, a pulled env file that pointed local schema pushes at the production database. The pre-push hook that protects migrations checks a list of schema files rather than whole folders, so editing a component never trips it and nobody learns to bypass it. That is a decision about behavior. A check people route around protects nothing.

In the loop I run now, each task starts as one line from me and lands only when I decide it is right. Agents fill the middle, and the middle got cheap. The two ends are design work, and they are the part of the job that grew.
The workflow is written up in [Fourteen branches, one afternoon](https://www.milesroxas.com/posts/fourteen-branches-one-afternoon-how-i-work-in-parallel-as-a-solo-engineer).
